Apple’ın hamlesi, teknoloji şirketlerinin otonom yapay zekâ ajanlarına yönelik yatırımlarını hızlandırdığı bir dönemde geldi.
Meta’nın Muse adlı aracının restoran rezervasyonu yapma, seyahat planlama ve haber özetleri hazırlama gibi görevleri yerine getirebildiği belirtildi.

Şirketin üzerinde çalıştığı teknolojinin, ChatGPT ve Muse gibi araçların Mac bilgisayarları kontrol etmesini sağlayan sistemlere benzer biçimde çalışacağı belirtildi.

Bu yaklaşım, klasik sesli asistanlardan farklı olarak yapay zekânın yalnızca komutları anlamasını değil, görevi başından sonuna kadar kendisinin tamamlamasını öngörüyor.

Bu kapsamda kullanıcı verilerinin korunması, hangi işlemlerin yapay zekâ tarafından gerçekleştirildiğinin açık biçimde gösterilmesi ve kritik işlemlerde ek güvenlik önlemleri uygulanması planlanıyor.

double quotation mark Overall, Anthropic’s New York Stock Exchange debut was solid, rising 17% on Thursday, however, the stock is now firmly in double figures and trading just above $91 per share.

double quotation mark The sharp price decline warrants revisiting the drivers of last year’s gold rally into 1Q26. Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famous hippopotamus, has died after swallowing a visitor's woolly hat, despite repeated attempts by veterinarians to save her.
The nine-year-old Nile hippo ingested the knitted cap last week after it accidentally landed in her habitat. She later began losing her appetite, prompting the zoo's veterinary team to provide round-the-clock care.

Asian markets record their worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI build out
Anthropic’s shares slumped at the start of trading on Friday, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Shares in the frontier AI company, which floated on Thursday, fell by over 9% at the start of trading on Friday. They dropped to $88.17, towards the $83 level at which the company sold shares in its IPO this week.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began.
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.7%. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell by 3%, after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
texts.https://www.wired.com/story/fiona-the-hi:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s famous hippo who charmed observers around the world, tragically died on Thursday due to medical complications after ingesting a knit hat that mistakenly entered her enclosure last week, according to zoo officials. Fiona was just nine years old when she died.
According to zoo officials, the hat that caused her death entered her enclosure after a child tossed it into the air. The hat reportedly collided with a ceiling fan, which then launched the hat through a “one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window." A few days after eating the hat, her condition began to deteriorate.
For nonexperts, Fiona’s tragic death raises several questions: Why and how would a knit hat kill a hippo that weighs more than 2,500 pounds? Why wasn’t surgery possible for Fiona? And for zookeepers, what was the range of treatment scenarios available?
Jan Hawkins, the head of the the clinical science department at North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, tells WIRED that—with the caveat that we won’t officially know until doctors conduct a post-mortem analysis—Fiona’s death was likely due to one of a few downstream effects of the hat getting caught somewhere in her intestinal tract.
In a sense, an intestinal blockage in a hippo is like a car crash on an incredibly long one-lane highway. Hawkins said that, estimating, a hippo’s intestinal tract is likely over 100 feet long, with more than 70 feet in the small intestines alone. In humans, the lengths of the small and large intestines are a comparably diminutive 25 feet.
Hawkins says that in a healthy hippo, liquids can take as little as 12 hours to pass, and food takes two to three days. According to zoo officials, Fiona ate the hat on or about Sunday, November 8. Zoo officials claimed that Fiona was asymptomatic at first, but began to lose her appetite after a few days. If the hat was going to come out, Hawkins says it likely would have happened within five days. So what happened?
One possibility, Hawkins says, is that when the hat got stuck, it caused a huge amount of swelling and pressure in her abdomen. That swelling could have led to her blood circulation being cut off, and eventually, to tissue death. After becoming green or black, Hawkins says that dead tissue is more likely to leak, and perhaps rupture, releasing the contents of the digestive tract into her blood. This can easily cause toxic shock.
In Fiona’s situation, this would mean that bacteria in her digestive tract died and released toxic molecules. Hawkins says that if these toxins enter the bloodstream, it would cause the organs to become more and more inflamed. Ultimately, this can lead to organ failure and death.
Another possibility is that, after the hat got stuck, Fiona’s intestines began to “twist on itself,” Hawkins says. This would be more likely if the hat, say, got pieces of food stuck inside of it, gradually becoming larger and heavier. Intestines are supposed to contract and move as they digest food. This means that if a heavy object gets stuck, the intestine can start to twist around it. In severe cases, this can cut off blood circulation. Eventually, this too can lead to tissue death. This initiates the chain of intestines leaking or rupturing, toxins entering the bloodstream, and organs becoming inflamed and eventually failing.
We don’t know exactly where the hat was in Fiona’s digestive tract. However, in a video the Cincinnati Zoo published to X on Tuesday, an unnamed staffer claimed that an ultrasound showed “some bunching of intestines.” They believed this meant that Fiona was “passing some things through her small intestine.”
If the hat was in Fiona’s small intestine, this would have meant that it passed through all three of her stomachs. (Hippos have three stomachs.) This could provide some hints about the type of hat that Fiona ate.
Hawkins says that in hippos, all three of their stomachs have the same basic components, but in different amounts. The first stomach has the largest amount of bacteria and protozoa, which help break down big pieces of food in the earliest part of digestion. The third has the highest amounts of enzymes and hydrochloric acid, which reduce food scraps into their smallest-possible size before entering the small intestine.
“Let's say it was a cotton hat or some sort of organic material, it's possible that that could partially break down,” Hawkins tells WIRED. “Whereas if it had something that would not degrade—so a plastic, or polyester, or something like that—then obviously its character is not gonna break down at all.”
The effects of this, Hawkins says, would be even more severe if the hat was rigid, or not collapsible in any way. “If it wouldn't get scrunched down, like a hair scrunchie, then you could understand why it would get stuck,” Hawkins says. “Because it can't change its character as much.”
All of this, Hawkins says, may have affected whether Fiona was able to pass the hat.
According to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video , conducting surgery to remove the hat would not be possible for Fiona. The zoo claimed that a combination of specialists—including “veterinarian human specialists,” zoo employees, and “other experts”—came to the conclusion that surgery wasn’t the best option, and that the “best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass this on her own.”
Rebecca Lewison—San Diego State University biology professor, and co-chair of the Hippo Specialist Group of the International Union for Conservation of Nature—tells WIRED that when it comes to hippo surgery, a major challenge is their “unpredictable and irregular responses to sedation and anesthesia.”
“It is very risky for [hippos], and they can die from the standard medication used on other large animals, like elephants and rhinos, for reasons we don't well understand,” Lewison tells WIRED.
There are also some inherent challenges to administering anaesthesia on an animal as large as Fiona. When a human or animal goes under anesthesia, they need to be put on a ventilator that artificially breathes for them. An animal that weighs more than 2,500 pounds, Hawkins says, requires a ventilator of a much different scale than what humans need for general surgery.
Fiona was placed under anaesthesia to conduct bloodwork, according to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video . But Hawkins says that the amount of anesthesia required for bloodwork is much smaller than what would be required for a major surgery, like removing a foreign object from her intestines. For Fiona, the increased amount of anaesthesia alone increases the risk of the surgery.
Another fact to consider, Hawkins says, is the position the zoo would feasibly be able to place her in while conducting surgery. If a human is in surgery, they may be placed on their back, their stomach, on their side, or in a variety of other positions. With animals like hippos, Hawkins says, this gets more complicated.
“You would have to have a hoist, a forklift or something, to pick them up to put them on either a pad or on a table,” Hawkins says. And if a zoo doesn’t have a table that’s big enough, the animal may have to go on the floor.
But Hawkins says that even at perfectly resourced zoos, there are other risks for hippos. In order to perform a major surgery, an animal as large as Fiona would have to have a huge amount of anaesthesia, putting her unconscious, and in the same position, for a long period of time. She would have her entire body weight putting pressure on the parts of her body that can’t move. This would limit her body’s ability to circulate oxygen—even with the help of a great ventilator.
If an animal is unhealthy, Hawkins says, the risks are even greater. In its Tuesday video , the Cincinnati Zoo said that when it recently ran some tests on Fiona, it found that she was dehydrated. This means that her body was already working extra hard to circulate blood not only to the blockage, but through the rest of her body.

Sean Cairncross is leaving his role as national cyber director after a chaotic week of tech outages. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will assume the position in an acting capacity.
Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United States over the week led to disruptions in air travel , banking and national security networks.
Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer, Kirsten Davies, as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity, media outlets reported citing White House officials.
"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.
"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.
During Trump's first stint in the Oval Office, Cairncross took on various roles as a White House insider. He was ⁠also an executive at ​the Republican National Committee before becoming the cybersecurity chief.

Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.
From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.
If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, Flowtica’s Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.
The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.
You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording.
The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk.
Priced at $159, the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to five meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table.
The companion app handles transcription and uses AI to turn recordings into more organized notes and summaries. Users also get 300 minutes of free audio transcription each month.
If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year).
Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier.
The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma.
Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital note-taking lineup, and also offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes.
Starting at $629 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas.
Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries.
If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you.
Priced at $249, this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls.
The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls.
Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday.
Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits.
The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window.

Over the past few years, WIRED has tested nearly every major brand of essential oil diffuser . Pura’s been our top nebulizer-style device (these work by blowing air through oil) for years due to its ease of use and sprawling library of high-end scents.
In fact, no brand even comes close to Pura's sheer breadth of available fragrances—with more than 150 options from big names like Anthropologie, Nest, LAFCO, Brooklyn Candle Company, Studio McGee, and more. Pura even has special seasonal collabs, like this month’s Nutcracker-inspired scents from the New York City Ballet . These diffusers are also highly convenient to use in that you can control them from your phone via an app (the Home, Plus, and Car also have buttons on the actual devices).
But, it's a luxury you'll pay for. If you own a Pura or have seen it in stores, you already know the scents aren't cheap; single cartridges range from $14 for Pura’s house line all the way up to $21 for name brands like Thymes and Votivo . (The prices displayed on Pura's website look lower, but that's only if you buy a recurring subscription—make sure you note the one-time purchase price.)
Cartridges can last for a month or more in the Pura Mini, but in a larger diffuser like the Pura Plus, they may only last a couple of weeks. That's why the best time to stock up on scents for the year is during a sale, like Pura’s Cyber Week event. Right now through December 6, all fragrances are 20 percent off, and all diffusers are 30 percent off.
Pura's diffuser lineup isn't perfect, but neither are any of the diffusers we've tried from any brand. Diffusers can be loud or messy, take up a lot of space, or have an uninspiring line of scents. Pura's Mini and Car models are worthwhile yet quirky (although I can't recommend the Plus), but the Home has given me no issues in six months of testing.
If you're in the market for a Pura diffuser, our top pick for most people is the new Pura Home. The first Pura I ever owned was the 3 model, and I've also had the 4, but the 5 (rebranded “Home”) improves on just about everything, with dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi compatibility; faster diffusion; control buttons on the device itself; and even a new way to load cartridges, where you can slide out the bottom portion (which is flat to sit on a surface), seat the scents, and click it into place. QR codes on the cartridges inform your app which scents they are and when they were loaded, so it can, in turn, remind you when it's time to replace them. I also like that this model is totally silent.
I also recommend the oval-shaped Mini—I have one in my office right now. Though you can only control it via Pura's app, scents last for over a month, and it does a great job at scenting a smaller space like a bedroom. My unit makes a high-pitched ringing noise, almost like an ultrasonic pest repellent, which is annoying, but Pura's customer service will likely replace yours if this happens to you.
There’s also the Pura Car, whose refills I will be purchasing during this sale ( MSRP averages $21 apiece , and the four-week run time has been roughly accurate in my experience). Online reviews of this device are mixed, but I love mine. If you’re a parent, having Pura scents to inhale instead of old, spilled food and stinky soccer cleats is 100 percent worth the spend. Buy one for a mom you know, but only if she has USB charging ports in her car—it needs to be plugged in most of the time, as it doesn’t hold a charge for very long.
Also on sale for 20 percent off is Pura's fun new Advent calendar , which features a Pura Home diffuser and 12 best-selling scents, most of which I have tried and can vouch for being options most people would enjoy.
Another Pura Cyber Week deal: Spend $50, and get 50 percent off the Pura Plus diffuser for large spaces , which has an MSRP of $80. I didn’t have the best of luck with the two Plus devices I went through—both eventually developed a loud buzzing noise. (Note that Pura will send you a replacement if this happens to you.) Additionally, unlike the Puras that sit flush to the outlet, this one is a cylinder that sits apart and must be plugged in at all times. It also makes an audible, fixed “shhhhhhh” noise as it’s long as it’s on (unlike the more intermittent noise emitted by competitors). However, it did do a great job of scenting a high-ceilinged room on the first floor of my house.

Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”
Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, and also by humiliating people.
According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate them with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him, and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.
Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

As talks are held in Brussels over closer relations, we examine the economic context and the challenges ahead
The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop.
Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
Burnham has said that Brexit “has not worked”, citing damage to the UK economy from leaving the bloc. However, there are also economic challenges facing the EU. Here we spell out the economic context behind the talks.
After the 2016 Brexit vote, years of political turmoil and economic uncertainty damaged business investment. Trade has also been hit by new barriers and red tape for exporters under the Brexit deal agreed by Boris Johnson.
Analysis by the economist Nick Bloom shows that UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a 4% hit over a 15-year period.
UK services trade has fared better. UK goods exports to the EU in 2025 were 14% below 2019 in real terms. Exports outside the EU were 8% lower. Services exports were 28% higher to the EU and 26% higher elsewhere, fuelled by Britain’s dominant financial services sector, as well as travel, accountancy, law, professional services, telecommunications and IT.
Britain has conducted trade policy independently of Brussels since Brexit. This has helped and hindered the UK in different ways. The government has been able to cut tariffs on certain products to help households with rising living costs – including gherkins in last month’s budget. The UK also struck a tariff deal with Donald Trump on better terms than managed by the EU . However, critics say the UK lacks the clout it had as part of the EU to sign international deals, and that sharply diverging from EU policies is undesirable. This is because divergence could undermine trading relations with the UK’s single largest trade partner.
The UK has taken a greater lead in AI adoption than EU nations, ranking third in the Global AI Index . France is the highest-ranked EU nation, in sixth. This is in part – but not entirely – down to the UK taking a lighter-touch approach to regulation than Brussels.
So far this year the UK has grown at the second-fastest pace in the G7, as AI bolsters growth despite headwinds from the war in the Middle East.
Brexit also had consequences for the EU, although as a larger market the changes have not been as profound. Barriers to trade have made Britain harder to access for EU exporters and migration has fallen.
Brexit gave a boost to populist political movements in EU countries. A wave of copycat exits did not materialise, with Britain’s political turmoil and economic uncertainty serving as a deterrent . But support for populist Eurosceptic parties remains, and battles over immigration, sovereignty and democratic accountability have not gone away.
The EU economy has faced similar global challenges to the UK – including from the 2022 Russian energy price shock and war in the Middle East. Trump has also aggressively targeted the EU in his tariff war.
Germany in particular has struggled from surging energy costs and Chinese competition hitting its industrial base. France has faced mounting political uncertainty, driving up borrowing costs and hitting growth.
Some EU economies have boomed – including former eastern bloc countries such as Poland, which has benefited from EU membership. Southern European economies at the heart of the 2010s eurozone debt crisis have also staged a marked turnaround.
The latest forecasts from the European Commission show that, as in Britain, the EU economy has proven more resilient than feared to the Middle East war. Germany has raised investment spending, particularly on defence, in response to Trump ripping up the western security consensus. AI-related investment has also bolstered activity.
For the UK there will be infighting over the extent of ambition for the future EU relationship. This could fuel uncertainty for businesses and take up political and civil service bandwidth that could have been deployed elsewhere.
Rejoining the EU would not mean a return to 2016. Some UK involvement in EU supply chains may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about British commitments to EU relations – particularly as the next general election draws near.
However, most experts are clear that there would be economic benefits from closer relations. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that rejoining the single market could grow the UK economy by 2-5%, equivalent to £61bn to £152bn by the start of the next decade.
The focus at this UK-EU summit will be on a youth mobility scheme , a food and drink trade deal that could add up to £5.1bn a year to the UK economy, and an emissions linking agreement that could add £3.8bn a year.
The EU will face a series of critical elections next year, including in France, Poland and Italy. Populism is on the rise and Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls to become the next French president. Germany does not have elections until 2029 but the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party is gaining support.
Early next year there also will be a test for the EU with the appointment of a new president of the European Central Bank to replace Christine Lagarde . That will come against a backdrop of rising inflationary pressures, slowing economic growth and pressures on government borrowing costs. The Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos is considered the frontrunner.
Britain is also expected to face a tougher year in 2027 due to the impact of high inflation from the war in the Middle East, with the squeeze on households also expected to weigh on growth.

Bondholders want SpaceX’s valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach.
Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.
The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.
SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.
It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.
The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.
The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.
SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.
The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.
The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.
More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.
Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.
SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.
Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.
The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.
“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.
“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said.

Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.
As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker . Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports . Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.
Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE said it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have launched on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With retirement of Falcon 9 on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a new rocket.
NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports . NATO launched two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.
Swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries — Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea —to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command and control networks.
Stoke wraps up booster engine development . Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the company’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke said. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.
All eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke announced it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims for full reuse of both Nova stages. The first launch is currently expected sometime next year.
Soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports . The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a new pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two launches per year.
What was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant says the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.
China’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster , Chinese rocket company LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News , a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.
But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The company did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.
SpaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports . It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and quickly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the company’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

Deals on food and animal goods, mobility and student fees have been agreed, but months of negotiations lay ahead.
The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow
Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.
“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said.
Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.
The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.”
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported.
He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK.
The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place.
Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia.
Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills.
“It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said.
“Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia.
Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.
“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”
​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.”
Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace.
He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones.
Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.
He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.”
Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine.
In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”.
In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 300 miles from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023.

Two sides find provisional compromise on scheme but food and farming negotiations go down to the wire
British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a concession to get the deal over the line.
The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.
On Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham , said the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He said: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”
But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.
On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.
The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards that France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.
Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year .
With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP , including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide . By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.
That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.
The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.
The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.
For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity .
But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.
The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.
Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.
Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.
Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.
None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.
Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.
Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.
The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?
The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.

Google, Gemini 4 Neon modelini tanıtırken OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra ve Sol modellerini kullanıma sundu. Apple ve Google'ın Mac bilgisayarlarda işlem yapabilen yapay zeka ajanlarına yönelik çalışmaları dikkat çekti. Meta'nın Muse ajanıyla ilgili gizlilik endişeleri ve California'nın OpenAI'a açtığı dava ise yapay zeka güvenliği tartışmalarını yeniden gündeme taşıdı. Microsoft'un yeni modelleri, Anthropic'in halka arz süreci ve yapay zeka girişimlerine yapılan yatırımlar da haftanın öne çıkan gelişmeleri arasında yer aldı.
Google, Gemini 4 ailesinin yeni üyesi Gemini 4 Neon modelini tanıttı . Karmaşık yazılım geliştirme, çok aşamalı görevler ve yapay zeka ajanlarının yönetimi için geliştirilen model, OpenAI'ın GPT-6.2 Sol ve Anthropic'in Claude Opus 5.5 modellerine rakip olarak konumlandırılıyor.
OpenAI, GPT-6.2 model ailesini Astra ve Sol ile genişletti . Yeni modeller, yazılım geliştirme, karmaşık problem çözme ve yapay zeka ajanlarının görevleri yerine getirmesi gibi alanlara odaklanıyor. OpenAI, modellerin güvenlik açıklarını tespit etme ve mevcut açıklar için düzeltmeler hazırlama yeteneklerinin de geliştiğini belirtiyor.
Google, Gemini'nin Mac uygulamasına bilgisayarda kullanıcı adına işlem yapabilme özelliği ekledi. Yeni özellikle Gemini, yerel dosyaları, masaüstü uygulamalarını ve web sitelerini kullanarak birden fazla adımdan oluşan görevleri gerçekleştirebiliyor.
Apple'ın Mac bilgisayarlarda kullanıcı adına işlem gerçekleştirebilen kendi yapay zeka ajanı üzerinde çalıştığı bildirildi. Sistemin uygulamaları açma, dosyalar üzerinde işlem yapma ve farklı yazılımlar arasında görevleri yerine getirme yeteneklerine sahip olması hedefleniyor. Yeni ajanın 2027'nin sonlarına doğru kullanıma sunulabileceği belirtiliyor.
OpenAI, ChatGPT'nin sesli dikte özelliğinde uygulanan 10 dakikalık kayıt sınırını kaldırdı . Live Dictation adı verilen özellik, kullanıcı konuşurken söylediklerini anlık olarak metne dönüştürüyor. Yeni deneyim, ücretsiz ve ücretli tüm ChatGPT planlarında iOS, Android, web ve masaüstü uygulamalarında dünya genelinde kademeli olarak kullanıma sunuluyor.
Microsoft, Ignite 2026 kapsamında kodlama, görüntü oluşturma, siber güvenlik ve ses teknolojilerine odaklanan yedi yeni yapay zeka modeli duyurdu . Modeller arasında MAI Code 2 , MAI Cyber 2 Flash ve MAI Image 2.7 öne çıkıyor. Microsoft'un paylaştığı test sonuçlarına göre MAI Code 2, Claude Opus 5.5'in kodlama performansının yüzde 96'sına, maliyetinin yaklaşık yüzde 5'iyle ulaşabiliyor. MAI Image 2.7 ise Artificial Analysis'ın görüntü düzenleme sıralamasında ilk sırada yer alıyor.
Alibaba, Qwen ailesinin yeni üst seviye modeli Qwen4-Max'i duyurdu . Şirketin paylaştığı karşılaştırmalarda model, Claude Opus 5.5'i 16 testin altısında geride bırakıyor. Bununla birlikte Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index'te Qwen4-Max 43, Claude Opus 5.5 ise 59 puan alıyor. Yeni model, özellikle kurumsal kullanım ve yapay zeka ajanlarına yönelik görevlerde rekabet etmeyi hedefliyor.
OpenAI, ChatGPT'nin performans sorunlarını daha hızlı tespit etmek ve gidermek amacıyla Performance Factory adlı yeni sistemini tanıtt ı. Codex destekli sistem, performans düşüşlerinin nedenlerini araştırıyor, çözüm önerileri geliştiriyor ve yapılan değişikliklerin sonuçlarını kontrol ediyor.
Google, Gemini'nin kullanıcılar adına işlem yapmasını sağlayan Tasks özelliğinin erişimini genişletiyor . Daha önce sınırlı sayıda kullanıcıya sunulan özellik, Gemini 4 Hydrogen modelini kullanan ücretsiz kullanıcılara da açılıyor. Gemini Tasks, işletmeleri arayarak randevu alabiliyor, Google Pay üzerinden alışveriş yapabiliyor ve kullanıcı izniyle web sitelerinde işlem gerçekleştirebiliyor.
Google, Gemini Notebook'a kullanıcıların notlarını ve belgelerini etkileşimli web sitelerine dönüştürmesini sağlayan yeni bir özellik ekled i. Kullanıcılar, yükledikleri kaynaklardan ders materyalleri, veri panoları ve proje takip sayfaları oluşturabiliyor. Hazırlanan siteler farklı kişilerle de paylaşılabiliyor.
Google, Gemini destekli Ask Maps özelliğini yeni yeteneklerle donattı. Kullanıcılar yapay zeka aracılığıyla kişiselleştirilmiş gezi rotaları hazırlayabiliyor ve kayıtlı mekanları için uygun rezervasyon seçeneklerini sorgulayabiliyor. OpenAI, yapay zeka ajanlarının kullanıcılar adına alışveriş yapıp ödeme işlemlerini tamamlamasını sağlayan ChatGPT Wallet'ı tanıttı . Kullanıcılar ödeme kartlarını sisteme ekledikten sonra yapay zeka ajanlarına ürün satın alma görevi verebiliyor. Her satın alma işlemi kullanıcı tarafından biyometrik doğrulamayla onaylanıyor.
OpenAI, kurumsal satış ekiplerine yönelik ChatGPT for Sales çözümünü duyurdu. Yeni sistem, Salesforce ve HubSpot gibi müşteri ilişkileri yönetimi platformlarının verilerini ChatGPT'ye taşıyor. Otuzdan fazla yeni ve güncellenmiş eklentiyle satış ekiplerinin müşteri araştırması yapması, toplantılara hazırlanması ve satış fırsatlarını takip etmesi kolaylaştırılıyor.
Reuters'ın şirket içi yazışmalara dayandırdığı haberine göre Meta çalışanları, Muse yapay zeka ajanının farklı hesaplara ait konuşmaları birbirine karıştırabileceği konusunda endişelerini dile getirdi . Bazı çalışanlar, kendilerine ait olmayan mesaj ve finansal bilgilerin karşılarına çıktığını bildirdi. Meta, test edilen sürümün kamuya açık üründen farklı olduğunu ve belirlenen sorunlar üzerinde çalışıldığını açıkladı.
California Başsavcısı Rob Bonta , OpenAI'ın yapay zeka ajanlarını yeterli güvenlik önlemleri olmadan test ettiğini ileri sürerek şirkete dava açtı . Başsavcılığa göre OpenAI, testler sırasında yapay zeka ajanlarının kontrolünü en az 80 kez kaybetti . California yönetimi, şirketin güvenlik prosedürlerinin mahkeme kararıyla değiştirilmesini istiyor.

OpenAI , NATO'nun İletişim ve Bilgi Ajansı (NCIA) ile yürüttüğü çalışmalarda gelişmiş siber güvenlik modellerinin kullanıldığını açıkladı . Avrupa Birliği Siber Güvenlik Ajansı ENISA'nın da OpenAI modellerinden yararlanarak çeşitli yazılım açıklarını tespit ettiği belirtiliyor. Diğer taraftan siber güvenlik girişimi Calif, OpenAI'ın GPT-6 Cyber modelinin yardımıyla Java'da ciddi bir güvenlik açığı tespit ettiğini duyurdu. Google Threat Intelligence Group , yayımladığı yeni raporda yapay zeka ajanlarının siber saldırılarda daha bağımsız roller üstlenmeye başladığını belirtti . Rapora göre saldırganlar, birden fazla yapay zeka ajanını birlikte kullanarak güvenlik açıklarını araştırabiliyor ve saldırı süreçlerini hızlandırabiliyor. Nvidia'nın kurucusu Jensen Huang 'ın CEO'luk görevinden ayrılmasının ardından şirketin yönetimine ilişkin tartışmalar devam etti. Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was visiting Poland on Friday, said: "The impact of Russia's illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday's incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Warehouses, railway stations, energy plants and residential buildings were hit during a night of heavy Russian strikes
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
At least two people were killed in a strike on a railway station in western Ukraine
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country .
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".
