A Myanmar government spokesperson said the ruling was unjust and noted that the court’s decision was not unanimous.
Myanmar’s government has rejected a ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that its security forces conducted state-sponsored genocide against the country’s Rohingya minority, calling the judgement “unfair”.
Myanmar’s government spokesperson Khaing Khaing Soe told a news conference on Friday that the military government was a victim of injustice. China also criticised the verdict, a day after issuing a statement alongside the United States and Russia calling on international bodies such as the ICJ to refrain from abusing their jurisdiction.
The statements follow an ICJ ruling on Thursday that said Buddhist-majority Myanmar had committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority in a crackdown in 2017.
“Our country was unjustly accused,” Soe said. “This ⁠⁠decision is not a ⁠⁠unanimous decision by everyone; it is not fair.”
China, which is allied to Myanmar’s military government, said that such rulings by the UN’s top court are “not conducive to the settlement of disputes”.
“The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
The ICJ found that Myanmar’s military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape and sexual violence against Rohingya women, and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called “clearance operations”.
Of the court’s 15 judges, nine ruled in favour of declaring genocide and six ruled against. It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges had determined that a state committed genocide.
One of the court’s judges is Chinese and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.
The brutal crackdown launched by Myanmar security forces nine years ago forced about 700,000 Rohingya to seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Some also fled further afield, including to Malaysia.
The ICJ’s ruling said Myanmar had an obligation to compensate the Rohingya for the violations it had committed, to be determined later, and it must also allow the “safe and dignified return” of Rohingya displaced as a ⁠⁠result of Myanmar’s “wrongful acts”.
On Friday, Malaysia said it plans to resettle 10,000 Rohingya migrants in Turkiye as part of efforts to resolve the long-running refugee challenge it has faced.
Rohingya people make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the United Nations.
Myanmar is in the grip of a multi-fronted civil war, including in Rakhine state where most of the country’s Rohingya lived.

The attack follows Putin’s pledge of ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.
Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.
The attacks overnight on Thursday into Friday hit vital transport bridges spanning the Dnipro River in the capital and knocked out power generation in several parts of Ukraine, officials said.
The missile and drone swarms came shortly after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation for Ukraine’s targeting of a symbolic bridge linking his country with the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.
Eight ⁠people – including six in Kyiv – were killed in the overnight attacks, and ⁠28 wounded, ‌Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said in a social media post.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles had damaged the Podilskyi, Darnitskyi, and Southern bridges, requiring traffic restrictions across the Dnipro.
Buildings, transport and logistics infrastructure were hit in several districts of the city, the Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement. Citywide electricity disruptions were also reported.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian sources reported that one person was killed as a strike hit a hospital in the Zaporizhia region. Nuclear ⁠power plants across the country were forced to reduce operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions, First Deputy ‌Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Friday that road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to ⁠the battlefield were targeted. It added that its forces hit defence ⁠industry facilities as well as energy and transport infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.
The large-scale attack came hours after Putin pledged a “painful” response to Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch Bridge earlier this week. The attack severed the key road link across the Kerch Strait.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters on Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin said the roadside of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and pledged to rebuild it.
Ukraine continued its efforts to target energy and military infrastructure overnight. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported that its forces had intercepted 310 Ukrainian drones.
A Ukrainian drone ⁠attack damaged an ⁠industrial facility in Russia’s western ‌region of Smolensk, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on the ⁠Telegram messaging app, ⁠without identifying ⁠the facility.
The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned ⁠Systems Forces said on Friday that 40 Russian oil ⁠facilities and defence ⁠industry targets have been hit over the past 50 days.
Moscow-installed officials in occupied eastern Ukraine also reported three people had been killed during an attack.
The overnight hostilities illustrate the lack of progress in US-led efforts to mediate a ceasefire.
US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia is comfortable with Europe joining the negotiations, and also with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine that are modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
Early on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said cooperation between Ukraine, the US and Europe on negotiations is “becoming closer” and that he hoped the US would organise the first multilateral meeting involving the Europeans “as soon as possible”.
Russian ⁠Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said ⁠later that ⁠a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia ‌is “under consideration”.
However, he added that any form of Ukrainian membership of NATO is unacceptable to Moscow.
“[E]ven the notion of a formula for Ukraine’s quasi-membership of NATO, and the search for some sort of – in inverted commas – ‘creative ⁠solution’ in this area, is an option that is ⁠unacceptable to us. We discuss security guarantees first and foremost in terms of ensuring the security of our own country,” Ryabkov was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency.
“As far as Ukraine is concerned, let ⁠them recognise the irrevocable nature of our demand ⁠that this state must not join NATO. When that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed in one way or another,” Ryabkov was quoted as adding.

Estonia formally approved the closure of all road crossings on its border with Russia from 1 December, in response to a sabotage attack on a defence company that Tallinn attributed to Russian military intelligence.
All five checkpoints — Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse — will be closed. The government said it may review the decision in six months. Rail services will not be affected.
The government described the move as "a response to Russia's ongoing hostile actions against Estonia and other European countries." Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia would "not allow Russia to use our openness against us."
The closure follows an attempted arson at the Threod Systems defence facility in Viimsi, near Tallinn, on the night of 14 November. Production and products were undamaged.
Authorities detained eight people from Latvia in connection with the incident.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced last Sunday that Estonia was considering closing the border, citing evidence that the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency, had ordered the attack.
Estonian defence companies have been targeted twice this year. The Estonian Internal Security Service said Russian security services authorised both operations.
Earlier this week, President Ülle Madise urged the cabinet not to act "under the influence of emotions," while acknowledging that keeping the borders open meant extra work for Estonia's security agency Kapo.
Estonia is not the first EU country on Russia's border to take such a step. Finland closed its land border with Russia in December 2023, and Latvia, Lithuania and Poland have significantly curtailed crossings at their eastern borders in recent years.
In practice, only three of the five checkpoints — at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula — were in active use before the decision. Russia suspended road traffic at Narva in February 2024, though pedestrian crossings remained open.
Moscow denied involvement in the sabotage attacks, and the Foreign Ministry slammed the decision as "Russophobia".

The case sets a precedent for establishing a state’s intent to commit genocide beyond explicitly written orders.
After seven years of deliberations and investigations, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its minority Rohingya population.
Thursday’s ruling by the United Nations’ top court in The Hague has been viewed as historic, the first genocide verdict it has handed down since it was established in 1945.
For the majority-Muslim Rohingya – 1.2 million of whom are languishing in cramped refugee camps in Bangladesh while more than 500,000 remain trapped and targeted in Myanmar – it marked vindication and international recognition of their suffering following decades of persecution, torture and killings at the hands of the Myanmar military and non-Rohingya rebel groups in their home state of Rakhine.
This judgement has given hope to other persecuted populations around the world. It now sets a precedent to establish a government’s intent to commit genocide – a difficult aspect of such cases.
Experts say the verdict has strong implications for South Africa’s genocide case against Israel over its war on Gaza, which is one of those pending at the ICJ.
Just as Rohingya people celebrated and cried tears of joy when the court’s president pronounced a genocide ruling three hours into his readout of the verdict, many are wondering if this is a sign that Palestinians, too, will one day be able to do the same.
“This judgement will not decide the Gaza case,” Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar, however, told Al Jazeera. “But it may determine the legal lens through which Gaza is eventually judged.”
On December 29, 2023, three months into Israel’s war on Gaza, South Africa filed an application against Israel at the Hague court, alleging that Israel was – and is – committing genocide against the Palestinian people living there.
Pretoria requested that the ICJ first approve emergency measures to protect civilians by immediately ordering Israel to suspend its military operations.
In two days of hearings in January 2024, the ICJ ruled that it is “plausible” that Israel’s actions could amount to genocide and ordered provisional measures requesting it “take all measures” to prevent the crime, despite Israel’s arguments that it was acting in self-defence following the deadly Hamas-led attacks on army outposts and villages in southern Israel on October 7, 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people.
In March 2024, after South Africa had requested additional measures in light of Israel’s continued mass killings in Gaza, the court ordered Israel to ensure that food enters the enclave, finding that Palestinians in Gaza were facing famine and starvation.
In a third order in May that year, the ICJ ordered Israel to halt a deadly ground invasion in Rafah.
Israel did not comply with any of these orders, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have concluded.
At the time of the hearings in January 2024, some 23,000 people – including 10,000 children- had been killed in Gaza.
As of now, close to 75,000 people have been killed in Gaza, including an estimated 21,000 children. That does not include the thousands of people who are still missing and presumed dead under the rubble.
At least 1,662 people have been killed since an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire agreement was announced between Israel and Hamas.
A verdict on whether Israel is committing genocide is expected to take several years as the two parties must submit written arguments and counterarguments. South Africa’s next submission will be in November 2027.
For both the Rohingya and Palestinians in Gaza, legal proceedings have offered little immediate solace: tent camps are being washed away amid intense storms for both refugee communities. Civilians are also still being killed – by continuing Israeli strikes on Gaza, most recently on the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza, and by violence against Rohingya in Myanmar from both military and rebel groups.
The Gambia accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya in November 2019.
That was two years after the Tatmadaw, Myanmar’s feared military, first began “clearance operations” that it claimed were a response to attacks on police posts by the rebel Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, which is fighting for Rohingya independence.
Myanmar denied committing crimes against civilians despite photos, videos and satellite images which showed mass killings and razed Rohingya villages, and despite gruelling accounts of torture and rape from thousands of survivors, as well as hate speech spread by senior Tatmadaw commanders.
On Thursday, nine of the ICJ’s 15-judge panel on the Rohingya case ruled that the “only reasonable inference” to be made from the evidence of widespread atrocities in Myanmar was that indeed, genocide had been committed.
The court said Myanmar had knowingly allowed civilian militias to participate in targeting Rohingya, failed to investigate or punish culpable commanders, acted with “intent” to destroy the group and prevent births, and violated provisional measures earlier issued in 2020 to preserve evidence.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
It ordered that Myanmar provide reparations and restitution by ensuring the safe return of Rohingya people to their lands, replacing damaged property and compensating those affected, accounting for missing people, reuniting families and ensuring dignified burials, providing medical and trauma care, and importantly, ensuring that such violations never happen again.
Such imagery and testimonies have also been abundant in Gaza, where 2.1m people are currently concentrated in a 128sq km area (35 percent of Gaza) behind Israel’s so-called “Yellow Line”. Israel’s far-right officials have also made numerous statements debasing Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
In 2025, the Al Jazeera Investigative Unit’s feature documentary, GAZA, also exposed Israeli war crimes through the use of videos and photographs posted online by Israeli soldiers themselves.
The court’s acceptance of evidence in the Rohingya case beyond just explicit, written orders from senior military figures has led observers to conclude that it could take a similar view in relation to the war on Gaza.
United Nations expert panels have already concluded genocide has taken place in Gaza, as has the International Association of Genocide Scholars.
Like Myanmar, Israel has claimed a right to self-defence, and says it is targeting Hamas, rather than civilians, despite the majority of casualties being women and children.
In its ruling against Myanmar, the court has demonstrated that intent to commit genocide can be inferred from cumulative patterns, Najar said. “The court must assess the evidence concerning Gaza independently, but [this ruling] provides South Africa with a much clearer legal road map,” he said.
At the centre of the Myanmar case lay the central question that defined the past quarter-century: whether a state may destroy a people so long as it describes that brutality as “counterterrorism”, Anas Mustapha of the UK-based advocacy organisation, CAGE International, said.
“Today, for the first time, a court has refused to accept that defence, and Myanmar has been held to account for a genocide it carried out in that language,” he noted, adding that the US and other colonial Western nations provided the templates used against the Rohingya and Palestinians.
“The governments that wrote the language, from the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq to the genocide in Gaza, have so far escaped any such reckoning.”
Genocide – specifically the intent to commit it – is much harder to prove than war crimes …

World Cup winners and European champions Spain have reached three of the four Nations League finals, winning in 2023.
World champions Spain will face France while England will play Norway in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League after the draw took place on Friday.
Spain beat France 2-0 in the semifinals of the World Cup in the United States in July on the way to winning the trophy . They also defeated Les Bleus 5-4 in the semifinals of the last edition of the Nations League last year.
The quarterfinals will be played over two legs in late March with Spain at home first after coming second in Group A3 while France topped Group A1 .
Spain won the Nations League in 2023 while France beat them to win the 2021 final.
England topped Group A3 on goal difference after beating Spain away in their last outing, and their reward is a two-legged last-eight tie with Norway with the first leg on Norwegian soil.
England edged Norway in the World Cup quarterfinals this year before losing to Argentina in the semifinals.
The other quarterfinal ties will pit reigning Nations League champions Portugal against the Netherlands and Belgium against Germany.
The winners of the quarterfinals will advance to the final stages, which will be held in June at a venue yet to be decided.
Spain or France will play the Netherlands or Portugal in the single-leg semis, and England would face Belgium or Germany should they get past Norway.

Iraq’s Federal Police are due to assume control of town’s newly established control headquarters.
Iraqi security forces have been deployed to Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the powerful Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah armed group.
Security forces arrived in the town, which sits in Babil province about 60km southwest of Baghdad and is also known as Jurf al-Nasr , on Friday.
The deployment, which is understood to have been driven by pressure from the United States and its Gulf allies, comes a day after a compromise deal was sealed that will see Kataib Hezbollah move to other areas of the country.
The government announced on Monday that it would take control of Jurf al-Sakhar after a probe raised suspicions that the group had stolen hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iraqi oil via illicit oil refineries.
It gave the group, which is believed to have thousands of trained fighters, a deadline of Friday to leave the town. However, under Thursday’s deal, they are expected to withdraw from the area within a month.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, has denied the allegations of stealing oil. Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following the investigation into alleged oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar.
Analysts suspect the push for withdrawal is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus. Baghdad has also come under pressure from the US to reduce Iran’s influence in the country.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has had to tread a fine line as he seeks to contain Kataib Hezbollah without triggering a confrontation.
Al-Zaidi said on Friday, as he addressed the government forces entering the town, that they were “not waging war”.
“Everyone present there are your brothers,” he told the troops, “the sons of this nation, and their blood is our blood.”
However, he insisted that his decision to restrict weapons to state control was final.
Under the compromise, a combined force comprising an Iraqi army brigade, a Federal Police battalion and an Energy Police regiment will provide protection for oil pipelines in the area.
Two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) Commission, a collection of armed groups that are part of Iraq’s official security forces, will also participate.
Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid said on Friday that a control headquarters had been established in Jurf al-Sakhar and that the Federal Police would control the facility, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
Iraq’s Energy Police have also begun securing an oil pipeline running through Jurf al-Sakhar, INA reported.
Baghdad-based security and strategic analyst Fadel Abu Raghif told Al Jazeera that the deal for Iraqi security forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar came after lengthy and delicate talks with Kataib Hezbollah.
The agreement followed “in-depth negotiations, and after wrangling and a tug of war that lasted about two months or so,” Abu Raghif said.
Highlighting the delicacy of the situation, Esmail Qaani, the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ Quds Force, had visited Iraq earlier this week to help defuse tension and seal the deal.
Kataib Hezbollah helped recapture Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) and has had a large presence in the town for more than a decade.
Reporting from Babil province, Al Jazeera’s Samer Al Kobeisi said the departure of Kataib Hezbollah would allow the reopening of an area that has been closed for about 12 years, according to the government.

The world watched with bated breath Thursday as the presidents of China, Russia and the United States met for 90 minutes for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen. Each leader came to the negotiating table with their own motivations. But Russia's Vladimir Putin was seen as walking away worse off than his counterparts, with some media outlets reporting the Kremlin leader was "humiliated" during the talks.
US President Donald Trump was welcomed with open arms when he visited Shenzhen, China’s “Silicon Valley”, from November 18 to 19 for a historic summit with his Chinese and Russian counterparts .
China’s President Xi Jinping went to the airport to welcome him, and he stood next to Trump in the official photo for both the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ( APEC ) summit and the opening banquet.
Read more What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
It would have been hard for the US president to receive a more rapturous welcome.
But Trump’s Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin , the third key player in this unprecedented summit, was treated almost like an afterthought.
While Xi and Trump embraced on the tarmac, Cai Qi, the Chinese Communist Party's fifth-ranking officia l, was assigned to welcome Putin upon arrival.
For the event's official photo, Putin was placed next to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan.
His seating arrangement for the opening banquet was equally lacking – opposite Liyuan, a former singer, and next to Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto.
Even one of Putin’s advisers, Yuri Ushakov, acknowledged that his seat placement prevented the Russian president from speaking to Trump and Xi during the meal, raising concern that these perceived snubs had ruffled Putin's feathers.
On Thursday, Putin kept Xi and Trump waiting for over an hour before joining the official opening of the historic summit that has been compared to the Yalta conference of February 1945 when the "Big Three" – Winston Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin – met to plan the postwar world.
"Putin usually likes to be late, and he has a history of this exact same kind of behaviour in diplomatic relations when things are not going his way,” said Jeff Hawn, a Russia specialist at the London School of Economics.

According to Natasha Lindstaedt, a specialist in authoritarian regimes at the University of Essex in the United Kingdom, the dynamics between this diplomatic "trio" resemble those of a mafia family gathering.
Like Don Vito Corleone in the film The Godfather – political heads of the "family" always make it crystal clear where someone stands in the hierarchy, said Lindstaedt.
"Authoritarian regimes do cooperate with each other, but they don't treat each other as equals," she said, adding that "some sort of jockeying for power takes place".
The series of diplomatic snubs directed at Putin did not go unnoticed by several Western media outlets and Russian opposition voices .
Putin "was put in his place", the Lowdown blog reported, in what the HungarianConservative referred to as "diplomatic humiliation" . Russian Telegram channel Vremennoye Pravitelstvo 2.0 claimed China sought to diminish Putin through "strange diplomatic tricks".
Before the summit, Putin had been referred to as Xi’s “ dear friend ”, but as talks began there was a stark change in attitude.
“There is a significant feeling, I think, in China that they're sick of Russia's conflict and they're unhappy with the recent ceasefire proposal on behalf of the Russians ... It shows no room for compromise. And that is irritating China because China's core objective always is increased economic growth,” Hawn explained.
By sidelining Putin in this way, Xi can ensure that he “establishes his dominance that he's the guy who Trump needs to talk to. Not Putin,” Hawn added.
Some experts said that Xi was generally frustrated with Putin, especially on the sensitive issue of North Korea.
“I think there was some irritation from the Chinese that Russia was getting so close to North Korea ,” Lindstaedt said.
China wants to maintain its influence over Pyongyang’s economic and diplomatic trajectory, a role that could be threatened by Moscow and Pyongyang's military-technological cooperation.
This new rapprochement between Pyongyang and the Kremlin could provide North Korea's Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un with an alternative political ally to China.
Xi can afford to show his displeasure because “Russia needs China more than China needs Russia”, Lindstaedt said.
Other experts suggested that the pomp and circumstance laid on for Trump was more to do with stroking the US president's ego than it was about dismissing Putin.
"Trump is there for ego and for the photo opportunity. Putin is there tactically, to show that he's not isolated and to try to continue to get leverage on Ukraine ... you have his (Xi's) attempt to show that China is the responsible power now," Scott Lucas, a specialist in US affairs and international relations at the University of Dublin, said.
In this regard, “the fact this summit is taking place is a win for him (Putin)", said Richard Turcsanyi, programme director at the Central European Institute for Asian Studies (EIAS).
On the other hand, Xi had to keep his distance from Russia to project the image of a leader above the fray, Lucas explained. Looking too close to the Russian leader, ostracised by much of the international community, would not have gone down well.
For his part, Putin must have suspected how the summit would play out.
“It was Putin's idea to have this trilateral ... Everyone understands, including Putin, that he is the weakest of the three, of course. So, the fact that he is meeting them as an equal is a win for him”, Turcsanyi explained.
“Xi Jinping and (Vladimir) Putin are meeting so often that for them, this is just another of many meetings,” he said.
Turcsanyi added that some media outlets may have exaggerated the “humiliations” the Russian president suffered.
He pointed out that several media outlets reported that Trump arrived to a rendition of the US national anthem while Putin had to make do with a Russian dance from Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s ballet The Nutcracker.
In fact, the Chinese musicians played “America the Beautiful” , which is not the official national anthem of the United States, despite it being a quintessentially American patriotic song.
Xi failing to greet Putin on the tarmac was no surprise, Turcsanyi added, since it is "not a common thing for Xi to meet foreign leaders at the airport".
China's president welcomed his US counterpart because “Trump met XI Jinping at the airport in the US last month”, and Xi may have simply wanted to return the favour.

Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.
Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying .
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes.
Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.
The latest official sales figures , external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.
"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.
"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."
The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September.
As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.
The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.
Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".
Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.
Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.
Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external
Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.
Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.
These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.
Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

The US Army says that detonating the unstable materials in place is the safest option to dispose of the degrading substance
The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.
The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.
The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.
On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.
The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.
The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.
On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".
The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.
The army said that the detonation is part of "a planned and controlled safety operation" to dispose of degraded lead azide. It added that the detonation has been permitted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under conservation and recovery laws.
Residents have been asked to leave their homes for about six hours - between 08:00 and 14:00 local time - while the operation takes place and the dust settles. The army said that "all humans" should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas.
Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations and will see a plume of dust, the advisory said.
According to Iowa Public Radio , external , the IAAAP found earlier this year that the lead azide - a highly volatile compound used as a detonator - stored in underground concrete tanks is degrading, becoming too unstable to safely move.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place is the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, said that the substance has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers.
It sits in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, but a routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the Associated Press.
The army said the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with barriers full of sand. The soil above will be saturated with water in an effort to reduce the lead in the air.
On Thursday, two environmental groups sued to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council.
"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."
texts.https://www.dw.com/en/myanmar-genocide-r:
The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Community members have hailed the ruling, but caution that achieving real change will be long and hard.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.
The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes , undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.
The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court , accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.
It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.
Lucky Karim was 14 when she and her mother and brothers were forced to flee their village in Rakhine State to escape the Myanmar military's advance in August 2017.
She joined the roughly 700,000 other Rohingya who crossed the border into Bangladesh at the time.
Now a prominent Rohingya activist, Karim heard the court's judgment in person in The Hague.
"For me … it's a very personal day, a personal moment, as someone who survived and escaped genocide in 2017. It took nearly a decade for the world to finally hear our voice," she said.
"For generations the [Myanmar] military stripped away our identity, our citizenship, tried to erase us from our homeland, told the world that what they did to us in 2017 was merely clearance operations, or worse, that we didn't even exist," said Wai Wai Nu, another Rohingya activist and former political prisoner.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Today, she said, their decades of persecution "is actually validated, and the truth has come out."
Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina , called the judgment "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya."
The press bureau of the Myanmar president's office did not respond to DW's requests for comment. The government's main mouthpiece, the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper, made no mention of the ruling online.
Throughout the trial, Myanmar claimed that its actions in Rakhine State were strictly part of legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group in the area that had been attacking police and military posts.
The ICJ flatly rejected the argument. "The court views casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, reading from the 15-judge panel's 9-6 ruling in The Hague.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," he added.
A UN-backed fact-finding mission concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. By some estimates, about 1 in 5 of them were children.
Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, said the court's ruling was both historic and "monumental" not only because it found a state responsible for genocide, but also because "it demonstrates that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible."
He noted that the panel took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the court's established "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent. The ruling also "helpfully affirms" that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors, he added.
Amid elation among the Rohingya and rights groups, the focus quickly turned to making the court's prescribed remedies real.
The ICJ said Myanmar was now obliged to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified" return of those who fled, investigate the crimes, and prosecute those found responsible. It also told Myanmar to return or replace all stolen property or, within two years, show the court it was compensating victims for what it could not.
But those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current president, Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021.
Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is still in the midst of a brutal civil war between the military and an array of armed resistance groups . And the group that now controls most of Rakhine, the Arakan Army, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well.
"These are not conditions amenable to realizing the relief ordered by the ICJ anytime soon," said Becker.
Enforcing the court's orders ultimately falls to the UN Security Council. But China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government and keep it well armed, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed Council resolution that aims to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.
"Whatever pressure there is will come from governments and the General Assembly, not the Council," he said.
Immediately after Thursday's ICJ judgment, the UK said it was expelling Myanmar's defense attache in London and would call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the court's decision.
A number of Western governments have already buried Myanmar under round after round of sanctions over the past decade, but with little to no apparent effect.
Myanmar is even taking tentative steps to shake off its global pariah status and restore regular relations with the rest of the world. Min Aung Hlaing has been warmly hosted by eight Asian and Eastern European countries since arranging his transition from army general to president earlier this year following rigged elections.
Horsey said the ICJ judgment would slow those efforts but not reverse them.
"Most governments in the region will keep engaging, but those with Muslim-majority publics, especially Malaysia and Indonesia, will find it harder to justify at home," he said.
Japan and South Korea, which maintain extensive business ties with Myanmar, are likely to remain cautious, he added, while the United States, which has reportedly had recent meetings with senior government officials, would keep up a transactional relationship.
"For [Myanmar], the real cost is that every government that deals with it will now have to explain why it is engaging a state found responsible for genocide," Horsey said.
The Rohingya, meanwhile, expect a long and difficult fight for real change.
"A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu. "It is imperative that the international community take action to enforce the ruling," she added.
Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground."
The Gambia's lead counsel in the case, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to help hold the perpetrators to account in other courts. The International Criminal Court, for one, is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity, also against the Rohingya.
Tun Khin said the wish of most Rohingya is simple, if still hard to foresee. "They want to return home, to their houses and own villages," he said, but this time with full citizenship rights and legal protection.
"It will take time," he acknowledged. "This is just the beginning."

As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a warming world?
For millions across the continent, climate change is no longer an abstract environmental concern debated in conference halls. It is already reshaping daily life, livelihoods and even decisions about where people can live.
In Zimbabwe , Harare resident Tsitsi Moyo says the effects are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. "The extreme heat wave we have been experiencing I think also has issues to do with rainfall patterns."
Jane Okello has witnessed similar changes in Uganda , describing increasingly erratic weather, including periods of unusually heavy rainfall associated with El Nino .
Their experiences reflect a wider trend across the continent. Communities that depend on predictable seasons for agriculture, water supplies and income are finding it harder to plan for the future as weather patterns become more extreme and less reliable .
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
For some, the consequences go beyond disrupted harvests or shrinking water supplies . Climate pressures are also influencing migration patterns. According to Professor Alfred Ngomanda, Permanent Secretary of the Gabon Climate Council, environmental stress can push people to leave their homes in search of more favorable conditions and more secure livelihoods.
Climate change is rarely the sole reason people migrate. However, droughts , floods, declining agricultural output and other environmental strains often intensify existing economic and social challenges, making displacement more likely.
As African countries prepare to make their case at the climate negotiations, Ngomanda stressed that the continent must emphasize the global importance of its natural resources.
"We will go to Ethiopia to assert that the Congo Basin is a stabilizing element for the global climate, and not just for Africans."
At the heart of the discussions at COP31 is climate finance, the funding used to help countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the impacts of climate change .
COP, or the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, brings together governments from around the world to negotiate action on global warming. The talks build on the Paris Agreement , adopted at COP21 in 2015, which aims to keep global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.
For African countries, the challenge is not simply making climate commitments, but securing the resources needed to turn those commitments into reality.
Opening the conference, United Nations (UN ) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted what he described as a fundamental injustice in the global response to climate change. "Developing countries face a double injustice: they bear the brunt of climate change but struggle to access the finance they urgently need," Guterres said.
The scale of the financing gap remains stark. According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the continent received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022, far short of its estimated annual requirement of $190 billion. Much of that funding also comes as loans, adding pressure to already strained public finances.
The shortfall is especially significant given that Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change .
African governments are therefore calling for funding that is more predictable, accessible and affordable, particularly for programs intended to help communities adapt to extreme weather, strengthen resilience and protect livelihoods.
African negotiators say the focus now must be on making sure that climate commitments produce tangible results on the ground. Speaking at a press conference on November 19, Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, lead negotiator for the African Group of Negotiators, argued that the continent needs a dedicated mechanism to translate climate proposals into funded projects.
"What we need is a mitigation implementation facility that moves Africa's proposals into actual financing and projects on the ground."
She said such a facility would help direct more resources to the continent while supporting economic growth, green industrialization and the development of Africa's critical minerals sector without driving up emissions.
Mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation involves preparing for and responding to climate impacts. African countries insist both are essential if the continent is to pursue development while coping with increasingly severe weather events.
Negotiations remain difficult. A revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19, removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion. While talks are ongoing and the text does not represent a final agreement, the changes underscore the political and financial battles that still shape international climate action.
For women like Moyo and Okello, however, the significance of COP31 will ultimately be measured far from the conference venue. Climate finance can support drought-resistant farming, improved water management systems, early-warning networks and infrastructure intended to withstand floods and extreme heat. But pledges alone will not deliver those outcomes. Countries must be able to access the money, implement projects effectively, and ensure support reaches the communities that need it most.

Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies
Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.
The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.
“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s Be Ready campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, the chief economist at the ONS.
Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month on month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.
Oliver Vernon-Harcourt, the head of retail at Deloitte, said: “Consumers responded to the government’s Be Ready campaign by stocking up on long-life grocery items, which reflects a broader attitude from shoppers to prioritise essentials.”
But Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics , said the jump in household “prepping” could mean slower food sales growth in the coming months.
“The cupboards only need to be stocked once for this, hopefully,” he told clients. “It seems unlikely that households can continue to spend at this rate with a further energy-induced rise in inflation around the corner.”
Separate data last week showed that British shoppers had been stocking up on essentials such as bottled water, tinned goods and hand sanitiser in preparation for possible emergencies.
The ONS also reported that textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost in October. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.
The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month on month in October.
Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.
However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.
“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, the European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.
“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.
“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

A 12-minute video of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session at Manchester United was leaked online, showing the new head coach doing training drills ahead of Sunday's match against Liverpool, live on Sky; the apologetic drone operator says he has now taken down the footage
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player
The drone operator who posted footage of Mauricio Pochettino's first training session at Manchester United on YouTube has said he has now removed the video.
The 12-minute drone footage over United's Carrington training ground showed the the Argentine overseeing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepared for their game against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports .
CC Overview, who posted the footage, said on Friday morning: "I would like to speak about yesterday's incident. A total error of judgement on my part led to me filming some of the Manchester United training session at Carrington, whilst the flight was legal in terms of drone laws I fully accept it was unethical on my part. My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time.
"I had wrongly presumed that with it being close to the start of the session that no meaningful training sessions would have started so would have been some harmless warming up shown.
"I also wrongly assumed that the training session would have been open to various media outlets. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.
"I would also like to state that Liverpool Football Club or any other football club were not involved in my decision to film at Carrington yesterday. The video has been removed from my channel.
"I have spent the past four years building up my YouTube channel and were well regarded in the fields I film and would now like to get back to building up my damaged reputation and making well-received responsible videos. Thank you."
However, the video has now been shared widely across social media. The footage has been viewed over eight million times on reposts from other X accounts and has since been reuploaded by several other YouTube channels, collectively attracting hundreds of thousands of views.
United have signs around the Carrington area warning that the use of drones is "strictly prohibited" and anyone caught "will be reported for prosecution and subject to civil action".
After the video emerged on Thursday evening, CC Overview maintained they had not broken any laws and claimed there were "many other media there".
Sky Sports News understands the club do not plan on taking legal action over the authorised filming of Pochettino's first training session in charge as head coach but will not rule out legal action in the future if further incidents occur to protect the rights of the club and its staff.
Sky Sports News has been told by club sources there was no security breach at the Manchester United training ground yesterday.
The club have acknowledged the drone operator has apologised and took down the footage without any contact from those at United.
Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola also reacted to the footage, saying: "They sent me it yesterday, the footage. But the important part of this is it shouldn't be legal.
"Yesterday you had access to our training, the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes of our training, you know who trained with us, you know who didn't train but it's not a matter of the advantage it's the fact someone can do this.
"There is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."
"This is quite an incredible story… this was a drone operator who flew not necessarily over the training ground or over Carrington, but far enough with a zoom that could really detail the tactical set-up that maybe Pochettino will go with on Sunday or what he's certainly working towards.
"You could also see the personnel who were there, questions around some players' fitness or availability… which ones were in place in his tactics run-through as well.
"This is a huge disappointment and not ideal for this Manchester United team who are trying to build some momentum, find some positive energy going into Pochettino's first game against Liverpool.
"It's just one win in 11 games in all competitions, and they're now having to get through another story and another burden.
"For Pochettino, it is now about protecting this group of players from more negative energy around them.
"Even before this happened, these types of incidents have been a concern for teams across the Premier League and EFL. Other clubs will be very aware and start thinking about how they can protect themselves from this happening to them.
"The footage has now been deleted, but of course it's across all social media platforms and you can't really take it back once it is out there, can you?"
"The only way to stop it is to reduce the airspace in the open category, which I guess the operator has been operating in. There's not much they can do. All the signage in the world isn't going to stop the operator from flying over.
"My view on it is that the privacy is there to stop people filming into homes. It's more of a legal debate as to whether filming a training session breaches privacy laws.
"There's lots of different sections of the law and the regulations. This guy seems to be operating in the open category.
"There's different certifications of aircraft. Different weight categories. The fundamentals are that when you're operating in a certain category you can't fly over assemblies of people.
"I don't know if that's the case here, but an assembly of people would be a group who can't move out of the way in the event of failure. On a sporadic training pitch, it's difficult to to say that a rule's been breached. Then once you're up in the air, you're in the realms of airspace. If there is no airspace restriction in that particular area and you're not near an airport, it's pretty difficult to stop that type of behaviour.
"I think the only way to stop it from happening is to increase security. Maybe buy more land because they can only go a maximum 500 metres away from the eyeline of the pilot. They have to remain within the view of the system in the air.
"If that's not a possibility, the only thing is to really restrict the airspace. That's up to the CAA (Civil Aviation Authority) on if they will allow that."

The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay . The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.
Environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi stands on a boat and looks out over the marshes where he grew up in southern Iraq. Despite having been kidnapped, tortured and accused by an Iran-backed militia of being an Israeli agent, Asadi is back in the marshes. Claire Harbage/NPR hide caption
Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.

Yaşadıkları zor anları unutmayan Murat Boz, kendisini ve ekibini kurtarmak için büyük çaba gösteren dalgıç polisleri İstanbul Deniz Liman Şube Müdürlüğü'nde ziyaret etti. Şarkıcı, o gün görev yapan ekiplerin fedakârlığını sosyal medya paylaşımında şu sözlerle anlattı:
"Sel felaketinin yaşandığı gün, ekibimle birlikte mahsur kaldığımız yerden sağ salim tahliye edilmemizi sağlayan kahramanları bugün ziyaret ettim. Bize ulaşana kadar bölgede mahsur kalan pek çok insanın yardımına koşmuş, son derece zor şartlarda, büyük bir özveriyle çalışmışlardı.
O gün gösterdikleri çabayı, sabrı ve fedakârlığı unutmak mümkün değil. Kendi canlarını riske atarak başkalarının hayatını kurtarmak için mücadele ettiler. Allah razı olsun. Bugün İstanbul Deniz Liman Şube Müdürlüğü'nde bizleri ağırlayan, o gün de tahliyemizi gerçekleştiren ekibin başında bulunan kıymetli Ertaç Özcan Müdürüme ve bütün dalgıç polis arkadaşlarımıza bir kez daha gönülden teşekkür ediyorum. İyi ki varsınız."

texts.https://tr.euronews.com/2026/11/20/james:
Artık yeni 007’miz var; 40 yaşındaki İngiliz oyuncu Robert Pattinson’ın Daniel Craig’den devraldığı smokini giyeceği resmen doğrulandı .
40 yaşındaki oyuncu artık, SPECTRE suikastlarından, köpekbalığı saldırılarından, stüdyo iflasından, COVID’den, alkolizmden ve muhtemelen birkaç cinsel yolla bulaşan hastalıktan sağ çıkmış bir karakteri oynayan seçkin bir kulübün üyesi. Üstelik serinin, 2007’de bir Bond filmi çıkaramamış olmasına rağmen varlığını sürdürmeyi başardığını da unutmayalım; o yılın pazarlama kampanyası kendini yazdı zaten...
Pattinson’ın 007’ye nasıl damgasını vuracağını ve Amazon yapımı bir Bond filminin nasıl görüneceğini söylemek için henüz çok erken. Bu yüzden, gelmiş geçmiş en uzun soluklu film serisinin mirasına dönüp bugüne kadarki 25 Bond filmini bir kez ve herkes için sıralamanın tam zamanı gibi görünüyor.
(Aranızdaki titiz okurlar için not: Evet, teknik olarak en uzun süren film serisi Godzilla; ancak kesintisiz ana seri olarak bakıldığında Bond hâlâ birinci sırada.)
Dr. No ’dan No To Time To Die ’a, kanonik olmayan Casino Royale (1967) ve Never Say Never Again (1983) filmlerini dışarıda bırakarak, işte sonuçlar, ki bazı Bond hayranlarını kaçınılmaz olarak çileden çıkaracaklar...
Özetle: Sean Connery’nin son (resmi) görevi, elmas kaçakçılarının izini sürmek, Las Vegas’a gitmek ve Blofeld’in bir petrol platformundaki planlarını bozmayı denemekle geçiyor. Baştan sona tam bir felaket.
Artıları: Parlak bir jenerik şarkısı; Charles Gray fena olmayan bir Blofeld... Aşağı yukarı bu kadar.
Eksileri: Aşırı kamp ama bir şekilde ruhsuz; Connery formdan düşmüş ve peruk neredeyse tüm oyunculuğu üstleniyor; tamamen boş kadın karakterler; son derece saldırgan klişelere dayanan eşcinsel tetikçiler Mr. Wint ve Mr. Kidd; serinin gördüğü en kötü senaryo.
Özetle: Pierce Brosnan’ın 007 olarak dördüncü ve son filmi, serideki en çok homurdanmaya sebep olan Bond maceralarından biri. Bond, gene terapisiyle Batılı görünüme kavuşan ve elmaslara kafayı takmış Kuzey Koreli general Gustav Graves (Toby Stephens) ile karşı karşıya geliyor. Cidden, elmaslar Bond için ölüm öpücüğü gibi.
Artıları: Bond’un Kuzey Kore’de yakalanıp işkence görmesi; Die Another Day ’in o kadar kötü olması ki yapımcıları aynaya uzun uzun bakmaya ve seriyi Casino Royale ile baştan başlatmaya zorlaması.
Eksileri: Nereden başlasak? Görünmez araba; tartışmalı beyazlatma; buz sarayı; dev lazerler; berbat CGI; Bond’un buzdağı üzerinde sörf yaptığı sahne; Madonna’nın rezalet jenerik şarkısı ve yüz kızartıcı cameo’su; Halle Berry’nin diyalogları... Kurtarıcı yanı çok az.
Önemli an: Judi Dench’in M’i, Bond’u görevden alıp ona artık "kimseye bir faydan yok" demesi. Ne kadar yerinde.
Özetle: Roger Moore’un James Bond’u, dünyanın en ölümcül suikastçısı Scaramanga ile, Solex adında maceracı bir isim verilmiş güneş enerjisi cihazını da içeren bir plan çevresinde karşı karşıya geliyor... Biraz da dövüş sanatları var.
Artıları: Scaramanga rolündeki Christopher Lee, Bond olarak Moore’un ikinci filmine sıkışmaktan daha iyisini hak ediyordu.
Eksileri: Önemli bir olay örgüsü unsurunun üçüncü meme olması; Britt Ekland’ın karakter gelişiminin sürekli bikini giymeye indirgenmesi; zaten ilk kez Live And Let Die ’de sıkıcı olan Sheriff Pepper’ın geri dönüşü; son bölümde adada geçen ve Scaramanga’nın uşağı Nick Nack’i canlandıran Hervé Villechaize’in de olduğu hikaye, yani özünde 007’nin "Fantasy Island"’a uğrağı.
Önemli an: Christopher Lee’nin altın tabancasını parçaları birleştirerek hazırlaması ve akşam yemeği masasında Bond’u gölgede bırakması.
Özetle: Casino Royale ’in bittiği yerden devam eden hikayede, Daniel Craig intikamla beslenen bir görevde 007 olarak geri dönüyor; Quantum adlı karanlık bir örgüt, Güney Amerika’daki su kaynaklarını kontrol etmeye çalışıyor. Bond hayranları arasında bu filmi yeniden itibar kazandırma çabaları olsa da, Craig’in 2006’daki Bond başlangıcının ulaştığı zirveye kıyasla hâlâ belirgin bir düşüş.
Artıları: Craig harika ve tam rolün adamı; yalın ve saldırgan anlatım tarzının bir çekiciliği var; filmin birçok kusuru, senaryonun 2008 yazarlar grevi nedeniyle tamamlanmamış olmasına bağlanabilir (bağışlanabilir?).
Eksileri: Jack White ve Alicia Keys’in pek işe yaramayan jenerik şarkısı; açılıştaki araba kovalamacasını ve at yarışı sırasında geçen umut verici yüzleşmeyi bile mahveden, nöbet geçirtecek türden çılgın kurgu; Mathieu Amalric’in canlandırdığı kötü adama ne yapacağını bilemeyen hantal senaryo; çölde geçen sönük final.
Önemli an: Filmin kapanışında Vesper Lynd’e yapılan son veda.
Özetle: Roger Moore’un sondan bir önceki filmi Octopussy ’ydi (arka sıralarda gülmeyi bırakın), Bond bu kez Hindistan ve Batı Almanya’ya giderek nükleer bir silahın çalınmasını engellemeye çalışıyor. Fabergé yumurtası da bir yerlerde önemli bir rol oynuyor.
Artıları: Öldürülen bir 00 ajanını merkeze alan sağlam bir başlangıç fikri; Louis Jordan ve Steven Berkoff’un canlandırdığı antagonistlerin büyük keyif vermesi; Maud Adams’ın kusursuz performansı.
Eksileri: Dönemine özgü egzotizm; Roger Moore’un asma dallarında sallanarak Tarzan çığlığı atması; timsah kostümlü Roger Moore; goril kostümlü Roger Moore; palyaço kostümlü Roger Moore.
Önemli an: Octopussy’nin sarayındaki final. Gülmeyi gerçekten bırakın artık.
Özetle: Başlığın da ima ettiği gibi, yüzük takan İlluminati geri dönüyor; dünya çapında istihbarat teşkilatlarının kalbine ajanlar yerleştirerek bilgi akışını kontrol etmek istiyorlar. Dünya hakimiyetini sağlamak için terör saldırıları da düzenliyorlar. Bu kadar umut verici bir fikir nasıl bu kadar kötü gidebildi?
Artıları: Ölüler Günü’nde geçen açılış sahnesi; güçlü bir ilk yarı.
Eksileri: Daniel Craig’li önceki filmleri kaba saba bir şekilde geriye dönük olarak birbirine bağlayıp Bond sinematik evreni yaratmaya çalışırken, Blofeld (Christoph Waltz) karakterini Bond’un evlatlık kardeşi haline getirerek heba etmesi gibi tüm umut verici unsurları mahvetmesi; dahası, Blofeld’in motivasyonunun çözülememiş baba sorunlarına indirgenmesi. Tam bir "Austin Powers" karikatürü. Belki tek kurtuluş yolu, Waltz’ı SPECTRE’ın "Bir Numara"sı yapıp, filmde heba edilen Monica Bellucci’nin aslında SPECTRE’ın gerçek lideri olduğunu, iplerin onun elinde olduğunu ortaya çıkarmak olurdu. İşte o gerçek bir sürpriz olurdu. Bir de, jenerik şarkıyı aslında Radiohead’in yapması planlanmıştı ve onların müthiş çalışması, yerini Sam Smith’in akılda kalmayan baladına bırakmak üzere çöpe atıldı.
Önemli an: Meksika’daki o "tek plan" gibi çekilmiş açılış ve ardından gelen helikopter dövüşü harika. Ne yazık ki geri kalanı, karmakarışık saçmalığa yuvarlanıyor.
Özetle: Bond’un uzaya çıktığı, Star Wars etkili bu macerada bir uzay mekiği hırsızlığı ve üstün bir ırk yaratma planı anlatılıyor. Sıklıkla en kötü Bond filmlerinden biri olarak anılsa da, aslında keyifli bir "köprüden önce son çıkış" eğlencesi.
Artıları: Megalomanyak Hugo Drax rolünde Michel Lonsdale; kamp tonunun çoğu doğru; sadece Venedik’teki gondol kovalamacası düpedüz "Looney Tunes" havasında.
Eksileri: Uzaydaki lazer savaşı; Jaws’ın (Richard Kiel) bir sevgili edinmesi (Blanche Ravalec); Bond’un MI6 ajanı olduğu gerçeğini tamamen unutan uçuk kaçık bir hikaye, sanki Luke Skywalker’ın karşı numarasıymış gibi davranıyor.
Önemli an: Boş verin, Jaws ve yeni sevgilisi için gerçekten seviniyoruz. İkisi adına iyi olmuş.
Özetle: Bond, Amerikan ve Sovyet uzay araçlarının yörüngeden kim tarafından çalındığını bulmaya çalışıyor. İpucu: suçlu, devasa bir yanardağ üssünde yaşayan Blofeld. 007, kedisini okşayan bu çılgın adamı durdurmak için Japonya’ya gidip ninja müttefikleriyle güçlerini birleştiriyor.
Artıları: Bond’un kendi ölümünü sahtelemesi; Ken Adam’ın tasarladığı volkan üssü; Blofeld rolünde Donald Pleasence.
Eksileri: Sean Connery’nin "yellowface" makyajı; Martini çalkalayıcıyla sallayabileceğinizden bile fazla sayıda ırkçı karikatür ve cinsiyetçi klişe; Connery’nin Dr. No , From Russia With Love , Goldfinger ve Thunderball ile yakaladığı dört filmlik muhteşem serinin a…

James Bond rolüyle uzun yıllar hafızalara kazınan Pierce Brosnan, ikonik karakterde bayrağı devralmaya hazırlanan Robert Pattinson'a destek verdi.
Yeni 007'nin kim olacağına dair uzun süredir devam eden meraklı bekleyişin ardından sessizliğini bozan Brosnan, Pattinson'ın fotoğrafını sosyal medya hesabında paylaşarak genç meslektaşına seslendi.
73 yaşındaki oyuncu, paylaşımında şu sözlere yer verdi: "Sevgili Robert, Bond dünyasına hoş geldin. Muhteşem olacaksın. Harika işlere imza atmanı ve her geçen gün daha da başarılı olmanı izlemek büyük bir keyifti. Bu yolculuğun tadını çıkar. Sevgilerimle"
James Bond serisinin önceki yıldızı Daniel Craig, 2021 yılında izleyiciyle buluşan 25'inci film "No Time to Die" (Ölmek İçin Zaman Yok) ile karakteri noktalamıştı.
Craig'in vedasının ardından yeni 007'nin kim olacağı sinema dünyasının en çok merak edilen konularının başında geliyordu.
Yapımcıların tercihinin Robert Pattinson'dan yana kullanılmasıyla birlikte yıllardır süren oyuncu arayışı da yeni bir sayfa açtı.
Süreç boyunca pek çok isim kulislerde konuşulurken, Pierce Brosnan da daha önce yeni Bond rolü için Callum Turner'ı desteklediğini ifade etmişti. Ancak kararın Pattinson ile netleşmesinin ardından eski 007'nin genç oyuncuya gönderdiği samimi mesaj büyük ilgi gördü.

Ünlü şarkıcı Murat Boz , İstanbul 'da ekim ayında yaşanan sel felaketinde kendisini ve ekibini kurtaran dalgıç polisleri ziyaret etti. İstanbul Deniz Liman Şube Müdürlüğü'ne giden Boz, zor anlarında yardımına koşan ekiplere teşekkür etti.
14 Ekim'de İstanbul'da etkili olan şiddetli yağış nedeniyle Sarıyer Ayazağa'daki Phoenix Stüdyoları'nı su basmıştı. Murat Boz ve Demet Özdemir'in de aralarında bulunduğu 200'den fazla kişi stüdyoda mahsur kalmış, bölgeye ulaşan ekipler vatandaşları botlarla tahliye etmişti.
Yaşadığı korku dolu anları unutmayan Murat Boz, kendisini kurtaran dalgıç polislerle yeniden bir araya geldi. Ziyaret sırasında kurtarma ekibinin başında bulunan Ertaç Özcan'a ve görevli polislere teşekkür eden ünlü şarkıcı, ekiplerin gösterdiği fedakarlığı unutmayacağını belirtti.
Boz, kurtarma çalışmalarında görev alan polislerin kendi hayatlarını riske atarak başkalarının hayatını kurtarmaya çalıştığını vurguladı. Ünlü şarkıcı, teşekkür mesajını "İyi ki varsınız" sözleriyle tamamladı.

England have been drawn to face Norway in the UEFA Nations League quarter-finals; the quarter-finals will be two-leg ties and will take place in the March international break; Wales will face Slovenia and Republic of Ireland will take on Croatia in the A/B play-offs
England will take on Erling Haaland and Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals.
Thomas Tuchel's side finished top of their group thanks to their dramatic 3-2 win over Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium, while Norway finished second behind Portugal in Group D.
The two sides met in the 2026 World Cup quarter-finals, with a Jude Bellingham goal in extra-time sending the Three Lions through to the last four.

Should England progress, they will meet Belgium or Germany in the semi-finals. The other two quarter-final ties have seen world champions Spain drawn with France and Netherlands take on Portugal.
The quarter-finals will be two-leg ties and will take place in the March international break, with the first legs between March 25-27 and the second legs between March 28-30.
This will then be followed by the Nations League Finals, which will be held between June 9 and June 13, 2027.
The tournament will feature two semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final. The four semi-finalists will be invited to make bids to host the semi-finals and final.
Wales and the Republic of Ireland have also learned who they will face in the Nations League A/B play-offs.
Wales avoided automatic relegation to League B after securing one of the two better last place finishers in League A, while Republic of Ireland finished runners-up in their League B group behind Austria.
Craig Bellamy's side will take on Slovenia, while Heimir Hallgrimsson's men will face Croatia.
The play-off ties will also take place during the March international break.
texts.https://onedio.com/haber/final-yapan-diz:
Kanal D 'nin Salı akşamı dizisi Haysiyet için 19 Kasım'da gelen final kararıyla birlikte sezon boyunca ekrana veda eden dizi sayısı yediye yükseldi. Eylül ayında A.B.İ . ile başlayan erken veda furyası Aşk ve Taht, Çirkin, Mercan Köşk, Sevdam Karadeniz ve Halef: Köklerin Çağrısı ile devam etmişti. Kararların hangi akşamın reytinglerinin ardından geldiğine tek tek baktık; bazı dizilerin bir önceki haftaya göre yükselişteyken, bazılarının ise ilk ona bile giremeden veda ettiğini görüyoruz.
Sezonun ilk final haberi, tamamen yenilenen kadroyla ikinci sezonuna başlayan ATV dizisi A.B.İ . için geldi. Dizi 22 Eylül Salı akşamı Total'de 3,32 ile dördüncü, AB 'de 2,42 ile yedinci, ABC1'de 3,07 ile altıncı sırada yer aldı ve ikinci sezonun 5. bölümünde final yapma kararı bu reytinglerin ardından verildi. Ertesi akşam ATV'nin bir diğer iddialı yapımı Aşk ve Taht'ın sırası geldi; dizi 23 Eylül Çarşamba günü yayınlanan 3. bölümüyle Total'de 1,62 ile 14., AB'de 1,47 ile 13., ABC1'de 1,45 ile 15. sırada kaldı ve 5. bölümde veda edeceği duyuruldu.
Çirkin'in sonu ise ekim ayının hemen başında açıklandı. Star TV dizisi 27 Eylül Pazar akşamı yayınlanan 10. bölümüyle Total'de 2,58, AB'de 2,60 ve ABC1'de 2,77 reyting aldı, üç kategoride de yedinci sırada kaldı ve kısa süre sonra 4 Ekim'de yayınlanacak 11. bölümle finale gideceği belli oldu. Ekim ayı ilerledikçe veda haberleri ATV ve NOW 'da da birbirini izledi.
Çirkin'in ardından ATV 'de sıra Mercan Köşk'e geldi. Dizi 3 Ekim Cumartesi akşamı Total'de 2,20 ile 8., AB 'de 2,06 ile 7., ABC1'de 2,22 ile 7. sırada yer aldı ve 7 Ekim'de duyurulan karara göre 7. bölümle ekranlara veda etti; final bölümü 17 Ekim'de yayınlandı. Prömiyerde Total'de 2,78 ile ikinci sıraya yerleşen dizi, birkaç hafta içinde sekizinciliğe kadar gerilemişti.
Mercan Köşk'ün ardından NOW 'da Sevdam Karadeniz çok daha hızlı biçimde yolun sonuna geldi. 12 Ekim'de yayına başlayan dizi, 19 Ekim Pazartesi akşamı yayınlanan 2. bölümüyle Total'de 1,84, AB'de 1,04 ve ABC1'de 1,58 reyting aldı, ilk 10'a giremedi ve final kararı bu reytinglerin ardından geldi. Dizinin 3. bölümü Total'de 1,25'e kadar indi, 2 Kasım'da yayınlanan 4. bölümüyle de ekrana veda etti.
Sevdam Karadeniz'in vedasının ardından NOW 'un uzun soluklu dizisi Halef: Köklerin Çağrısı da listeye dahil oldu ve bu, yedi dizi içinde en çok bölüm yayınlamış isim olarak öne çıktı. 5 Kasım Perşembe akşamı yayınlanan 41. bölüm Total'de 4,07 ile yedinci, AB 'de 2,87 ile yine yedinci, ABC1'de ise 3,37 ile dokuzuncu sırada yer aldı; final kararı bu reytinglerin ardından, 6 Kasım'da duyuruldu. İlk sezonunda Total'de 8,69'a kadar çıkan dizi, 19 Kasım Perşembe günü yayınlanan 43. bölümle ekranlara veda etti.

Türkiye Cumhuriyet Merkez Bankası (TCMB), yılın üçüncü çeyreğine ilişkin "Türkiye Dış Borç İstatistikleri"ni yayımladı.
Buna göre, Türkiye'nin toplam brüt dış borç stoku, yılın üçüncü çeyreğinde bir önceki çeyreğe göre yüzde 1,4 artarak 549,2 milyar dolara çıktı.
Aynı dönemde kısa vadeli dış borçlar yüzde 1,5 artışla 173,1 milyar dolar, uzun vadeli dış borçlar ise yüzde 1,4 artışla 376,1 milyar dolar oldu.
Alt sektörler itibarıyla bir önceki çeyreğe kıyasla kamu sektörü borcu yüzde 1,2 yükselerek 203,8 milyar dolara, özel sektör borcu yüzde 1,7 artarak 322,2 milyar dolara, TCMB'nin dış yükümlülükleri ise yüzde 0,5 artarak 23,2 milyar dolara yükseldi.
Dış borç stokunun enstrüman dağılımında en büyük pay yüzde 46,5 ile kredilere ait bulunuyor.
